## Functions of several variables

### Exercise 4.1

Find and describe the domain of $f(x,y)=\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}/(x-y)$. Identify which parts of the boundary circle belong to the domain.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
For the square root to be real, $9-x^2-y^2\geq0$, or $x^2+y^2\leq9$. The denominator must also be nonzero, so $x\ne y$. Thus
$$D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\leq9\text{ and }x\ne y\}.$$
Geometrically, this is the closed disk of radius $3$ with the line segment $y=x$ removed. Points on the boundary circle are included except where $y=x$. Solving $2x^2=9$ gives the two excluded boundary points $(3/\sqrt2,3/\sqrt2)$ and $(-3/\sqrt2,-3/\sqrt2)$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4.2

For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, describe the level curves $f(x,y)=1$, $f(x,y)=4$, and $f(x,y)=9$. What does the spacing between them say about the rate of change along the positive $x$-axis?

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Setting $f=c$ gives $x^2+y^2=c$, a circle centered at the origin with radius $\sqrt c$. The three level curves have radii $1$, $2$, and $3$. Their radial spacing is one unit for each increase of the level by $3$ and then $5$, respectively. Along the positive $x$-axis, $f(x,0)=x^2$, whose derivative is $2x$. Hence the rate of increase grows as we move outward; equal outward steps produce larger changes in $f$.
:::
::::

## Limits and Continuity

### Exercise 4.3

Determine whether $\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ exists. Compare two paths.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Along the $x$-axis, $y=0$ and the quotient is $0$, so the limit along that path is $0$. Along the line $y=x$, for $x\ne0$,
$$\frac{x\cdot x}{x^2+x^2}=\frac{x^2}{2x^2}=\frac12.$$
The path limits differ, so there is no single limit as $(x,y)\to(0,0)$. Defining any value at the origin could not make this function continuous there.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4.4

Let $g(x,y)=x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ away from $(0,0)$ and $g(0,0)=0$. Prove that $g$ is continuous at the origin.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
For $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$, since $x^2\leq x^2+y^2$,
$$|g(x,y)|=|y|\frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}\leq|y|\leq\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.$$
As $(x,y)\to(0,0)$, the right-hand side tends to $0$. The squeeze theorem gives $\lim g(x,y)=0=g(0,0)$, which is the definition of continuity at the origin.
:::
::::

## Partial derivatives

### Exercise 4.5

For $f(x,y)=x^2y+e^{xy}$, find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ and evaluate both at $(1,0)$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Hold $y$ fixed when differentiating with respect to $x$, and apply the chain rule to $e^{xy}$:
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2xy+ye^{xy}.$$
Hold $x$ fixed when differentiating with respect to $y$:
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=x^2+xe^{xy}.$$
At $(1,0)$, $e^{xy}=e^0=1$, so $\left.\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(1,0)}=0$ and $\left.\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(1,0)}=1+1=2$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4.6

For $f(x,y)=\ln(x^2+y^2)$, calculate $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}$ wherever the function is defined. Evaluate them at $(1,1)$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
The domain excludes $(0,0)$. First derivatives are
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\frac{2x}{x^2+y^2},\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{2y}{x^2+y^2}.$$
Differentiate $\partial f/\partial x$ with respect to $y$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ with respect to $x$:
$$\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}=-\frac{4xy}{(x^2+y^2)^2},\qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}=-\frac{4xy}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.$$
They agree, as expected for a smooth function on its domain. At $(1,1)$ each equals $-4/(2^2)=-1$.
:::
::::

## Tangent planes and linear approximation

### Exercise 4.7

Find the tangent plane to $z=x^2+xy+y^2$ at $(x,y)=(1,2)$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
The surface height is $f(1,2)=1+2+4=7$. Its partial derivatives are
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2x+y,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=x+2y.$$
At $(1,2)$, their values are $4$ and $5$. The tangent plane is therefore $z=7+4(x-1)+5(y-2)$, equivalently $z=4x+5y-7$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4.8

Use a linear approximation at $(1,1)$ to estimate $\sqrt{4+(1.02)^2+(0.97)^2}$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Let $f(x,y)=\sqrt{4+x^2+y^2}$. At $(1,1)$, $f=\sqrt6$. The partial derivatives are
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{4+x^2+y^2}},\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{4+x^2+y^2}},$$
so both equal $1/\sqrt6$ at $(1,1)$. The changes are $\Delta x=0.02$ and $\Delta y=-0.03$. Therefore
$$f(1.02,0.97)\approx f(1,1)+\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(1,1)}\Delta x+\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(1,1)}\Delta y
=\sqrt6+\frac{0.02-0.03}{\sqrt6}
=\sqrt6-\frac{0.01}{\sqrt6}\approx2.4454.$$
:::
::::

## The chain rule

### Exercise 4.9

Let $z=x^2y$, with $x=t^2$ and $y=\sin t$. Use the multivariable chain rule to find $dz/dt$ at $t=1$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
The chain rule gives $\dfrac{dz}{dt}=\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\dfrac{dx}{dt}+\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\dfrac{dy}{dt}$. Here $\partial z/\partial x=2xy$, $\partial z/\partial y=x^2$, $dx/dt=2t$, and $dy/dt=\cos t$. Substituting $x=t^2$ and $y=\sin t$ gives
$$\frac{dz}{dt}=(2t^2\sin t)(2t)+(t^2)^2\cos t=4t^3\sin t+t^4\cos t.$$
At $t=1$, the answer is $4\sin1+\cos1$. Directly differentiating $z=t^4\sin t$ gives the same result.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4.10

Let $z=e^{xy}$, $x=u+v$, and $y=u-v$. Find $\partial z/\partial u$ and $\partial z/\partial v$, then evaluate both at $(u,v)=(1,2)$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Since $\partial z/\partial x=ye^{xy}$ and $\partial z/\partial y=xe^{xy}$, the chain rule gives
$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}=(x+y)e^{xy}=2u e^{u^2-v^2},$$
because $\partial x/\partial u=\partial y/\partial u=1$ and $xy=(u+v)(u-v)=u^2-v^2$. Similarly, $\partial x/\partial v=1$ and $\partial y/\partial v=-1$, so
$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}=(y-x)e^{xy}=-2v e^{u^2-v^2}.$$
At $(1,2)$, $u^2-v^2=-3$. Thus $\left.\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right|_{(1,2)}=2e^{-3}$ and $\left.\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right|_{(1,2)}=-4e^{-3}$.
:::
::::

## Maximum and minimum values

### Exercise 4.11

Find the global minimum of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-4x+6y$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Does it have a global maximum?

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Complete the square in each variable:
$$f(x,y)=(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2-13.$$
Both squares are nonnegative and vanish together only at $(2,-3)$. Hence the global minimum is $-13$ at $(2,-3)$. As $x$ or $y$ grows without bound, the sum of squares grows without bound, so no global maximum exists on $\mathbb R^2$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4.12

Find the absolute maximum and minimum of $f(x,y)=xy$ on the closed disk $x^2+y^2\leq4$. Explain why the interior critical point is not an extremum.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
The disk is compact and $f$ is continuous, so absolute extrema exist. Inside the disk, $\partial f/\partial x=y$ and $\partial f/\partial y=x$ vanish together only at $(0,0)$, where $f=0$. Nearby points with $x=y>0$ have $xy>0$, while points with $x=-y>0$ have $xy<0$, so the origin is a saddle point.

On the boundary $x^2+y^2=4$, the inequalities $(x-y)^2\geq0$ and $(x+y)^2\geq0$ give $-2\leq xy\leq2$. Equality $xy=2$ occurs at $(\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$ and $(-\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)$. Equality $xy=-2$ occurs at $(\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)$ and $(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$. Thus the absolute maximum is $2$ and the absolute minimum is $-2$.
:::
::::
